title: Swing and Big Bands
objective: After this level you can describe the swing era.
summary: Swing-era big bands played brass, woodwind and rhythm sections off each other. Fletcher Henderson's charts shaped Benny Goodman's sound; Goodman's integrated groups crossed the color line.

cards.headline: The "King of Swing" got his band's sound from a Black bandleader's pen.
cards.body: Clarinetist Benny Goodman was billed as the King of Swing. Yet his band's most characteristic sound came from arrangements by Fletcher Henderson, a Black pianist and bandleader. In a segregated country, that partnership says a lot about the swing era: who made the music, and who got top billing.

cards.headline: A big band is three bands in conversation
cards.body: The swing era ran from about 1935 to the mid-1940s, when big dance bands were at their most popular. Arrangers grouped players into sections of brass, woodwinds and rhythm, then played the sections off against each other: one tosses a phrase, another answers. Hear the echo of Level 61's call-and-response? It's the same shape, now scored for a whole band.

cards.headline: What makes it swing?
cards.body: Swing isn't just a speed. Britannica describes it as a compelling momentum that comes from how players attack and accent notes against the fixed beat. The beat stays steady, just like Level 4's pulse; the notes lean on it and push against it. That forward pull is made for moving, and swing went hand in hand with African American social dances like the lindy hop.

cards.headline: Henderson's charts, and a color line crossed
cards.body: Fletcher Henderson's bands of the 1920s were especially important in spreading the ideas swing was built on, and his charts gave Goodman's band its most characteristic sound. Goodman also hired pianist Teddy Wilson, though he feared the consequences, and Lionel Hampton in 1936. In a time of segregation, those integrated groups gave Black musicians greater visibility.

questions.prompt: Whose arrangements gave Benny Goodman's band its most characteristic sound?

options.label: Louis Armstrong's
options.rationale: Armstrong was a trumpeter and bandleader, not Goodman's arranger.

options.label: Scott Joplin's
options.rationale: Joplin was a ragtime composer who died in 1917.

options.label: Teddy Wilson's
options.rationale: Wilson played piano in Goodman's small groups.

questions.explanation: Henderson, a Black pianist and bandleader, wrote the charts behind Goodman's sound.

questions.prompt: According to Britannica, what gives swing its feel?

options.label: Momentum from accents against a steady beat
Playing every tune as fast as possible
options.rationale: Swing is about how notes sit on the beat, not raw speed.

options.label: Using only minor chords throughout
options.rationale: Swing is a rhythmic feel, not a harmony.

options.label: Dropping the steady beat altogether
options.rationale: The beat stays fixed; notes push against it.

questions.explanation: Swing is a compelling momentum from attack and accent against fixed beats.

questions.prompt: From Level 44: what do swing and Chopin's rubato have in common?

options.label: The tempo gradually speeds up from start to finish
options.rationale: In both, the underlying beat stays steady.

options.label: Every note falls exactly on the beat
options.rationale: Both lean away from the beat without breaking it.

options.label: A steady beat, with notes leaning against it
Both were written for solo piano in small rooms
options.rationale: Swing was big-band dance music; the link is the steady beat.

questions.explanation: Swing's notes push against a fixed beat, and in Chopin's rubato the melody bends while the left hand keeps a fairly steady tempo.
